summary: Describes a way for an SSH client and server to agree on a shared secret using RSA public-key encryption instead of Diffie-Hellman. It needs much less computing time on the client, which helps slow devices. It is a proposed standard from 2006.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people need a secret code word. Instead of a slow back-and-forth puzzle, one locks the word in a box only the other can open. That is faster for a slow little computer.

questions: faster ssh key exchange for slow clients
what is ssh rsa key exchange
what is the ssh exchange hash
subtitle: A faster SSH key exchange that lets a slow client lock a random secret to the server's temporary RSA key.

tldr.problem: The core SSH protocol uses Diffie-Hellman key exchange, which on slow CPUs can take tens of seconds to complete.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a transient RSA public key, the client encrypts a random secret to it, and the server signs the resulting exchange hash with its host key.
tldr.outcome: The client does an order of magnitude less CPU work than with Diffie-Hellman, which suits mobile and other slow devices. RFC 9142 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 4432 is a Proposed Standard from March 2006 and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 9142. Read the update alongside this RFC.

sections.title: Why Another Key Exchange
sections.content:
The core Secure Shell (SSH) protocol of RFC 4251 uses Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The RFC says that on slow CPUs this exchange can take tens of seconds, which can be irritating for the user.

The older SSH version described in the RFC's reference [SSH1] used an RSA-based exchange that took an order of magnitude less client CPU time. RFC 4432 brings a similar method to the newer protocol, about as fast as the old one, while keeping the security advantages of the newer protocol. It is aimed at slow client systems such as mobile devices.
sections.plainLanguage: A slow computer gets tired doing the usual secret-sharing puzzle. This RFC gives it an easier way to do the same job.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
The method has three messages. The server sends the client an RSA public key called K_T, for which it holds the private key. It can be a transient key made just for this connection, or it can be reused for several connections.

The client makes a string of random bytes, K, encrypts it with K_T and sends it back. The server decrypts it. Both sides then hash K, K_T and the other exchange parameters to get the exchange hash H, which is used to derive the session encryption keys. The server signs H with its host key, and the client checks that host key as described in Section 8 of RFC 4253.

The method gives explicit server identification and requires a host key that can sign.
sections.plainLanguage: The server hands out an open padlock. The client puts a secret in a box, snaps the padlock shut and sends it back. Only the server has the key. Then the server signs its name to prove it is really the server.

sections.title: The Three Messages
sections.content:
The server starts with SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_PUBKEY, which carries the server's host key and certificates (K_S) and the transient key K_T. K_T is encoded in the ssh-rsa format of RFC 4253, but it is used only for encryption, never for signing. Its modulus MUST be at least MINKLEN bits long.

The client replies with SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_SECRET, holding the encrypted shared secret. The server decrypts it. If decryption fails, the server SHOULD send SSH_MESSAGE_DISCONNECT with reason code SSH_DISCONNECT_KEY_EXCHANGE_FAILED and MUST disconnect. Otherwise it answers with SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_DONE, carrying its signature of H made with the host key.
sections.plainLanguage: It takes three notes: the server sends the padlock, the client sends back the locked box, and the server sends a signed receipt.

sections.title: The Secret and the Exchange Hash
sections.content:
The client picks a random integer K that is smaller than 2^(KLEN-2*HLEN-49), where KLEN is the length of the modulus of K_T in bits. This keeps the encoded secret small enough to fit. Appendix A of the RFC gives a short proof that it always fits. The client encrypts K with the RSAES-OAEP scheme of RFC 3447, using MGF1 with the chosen hash and an empty label.

The exchange hash H is the hash of the client and server identification strings, the payloads of both SSH_MSG_KEXINIT messages, the host key K_S, the transient key K_T, the encrypted secret and K itself. It SHOULD be kept secret.

The signature algorithm MUST be applied over H, not the original data. When the signature scheme also hashes (for example ssh-dss specifies SHA-1), the data is hashed once to get H and H is hashed again when it is signed.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret is kept small enough to fit in the box. Everything said so far is then squashed into a short fingerprint, and the server signs that fingerprint.

sections.title: The Two Defined Methods
sections.content:
The method is parameterised by HASH (the hash algorithm), HLEN (its output length in bits) and MINKLEN (the minimum transient RSA modulus length in bits). The RFC defines two named methods.

  • rsa1024-sha1 uses SHA-1, HLEN 160 and MINKLEN 1024.
  • rsa2048-sha256 uses SHA-256, HLEN 256 and MINKLEN 2048.

The message numbers are 30 for SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_PUBKEY, 31 for SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_SECRET and 32 for SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_DONE.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a smaller, lighter version of the padlock and a bigger, stronger one. You pick which one to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If the server's transient RSA private key is revealed, the session key is revealed. The server should erase the key from memory as soon as it is not needed, and SHOULD use each RSA key for as few key exchanges as possible. If one key serves many connections, an attacker who finds the private key gets all of those sessions.

The key K_T should not be used as a host key, since RFC 3447 recommends that RSAES-OAEP keys not be used with other schemes. The RFC stresses randomness: it is essential that the client use a high-quality cryptographic pseudo-random number generator for K, and a bad one lets an attacker break all the encryption and integrity protection of the SSH transport layer.

Unlike Diffie-Hellman, this method lets the client fully choose the shared secret. The RFC believes this is not significant because K is only used when hashed with data the server partly supplies. Protocol extensions that use K directly should be viewed with extreme suspicion. The design also resists collision attacks on the exchange hash, since neither side can freely choose its input after seeing the other's.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone steals the server's key, they can open every box that was locked with it, so the server should throw the key away fast. And the client must pick its secret truly at random, or a sneaky person could guess it.

sections.title: Registered Names
sections.content: IANA assigned the names rsa1024-sha1 and rsa2048-sha256 as Key Exchange Method Names, in accordance with RFC 4250. These are the names a client and server use to agree on which method to run.
sections.plainLanguage: The two versions of the method were put in an official list so everyone calls them by the same names.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_SECRET
messages.note: The random secret K encrypted with K_T.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXRSA_DONE
